scope: Candidate reference images for late episodes c.177–258 involving Lugdunum/Lyon and Carthage. Commons original-description pages and license clauses were checked; three resized 1280-pixel JPEGs downloaded to /tmp only.

assets.author: Jean-Christophe BENOIST (Commons username)
assets.limitations: Photo depicts the surviving Roman theatre at Fourvière, not the 2nd/3rd-century church or martyrdom events themselves. Lugdunum museum’s official page says the structure was modified over time, later quarried, and excavated/partly reconstructed in the first half of the 20th century (https://lugdunum.grandlyon.com/un-musee-de-sites/roman-theaters). Use as modern archaeological-site reference only; not an ancient intact appearance. Credit author, license and indicate edits.
assets.usage: Modern archaeological research reference only; never a period reconstruction or historic-event depiction.

assets.author: Виктор Пинчук (Viktor Pinchuk)
assets.limitations: Modern panoramic photograph of the remains identified as the Antonine baths; wide crop/panorama, current ruins and conservation state, not a reconstruction of 177–258 urban fabric. UNESCO identifies Antonin baths among Roman-era components of the multi-period site (https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/37/); image metadata does not state a precise ancient construction phase. Do not imply the full modern visible footprint existed throughout episode dates. Credit author, license and indicate edits.

assets.author: Noomen9
assets.limitations: Modern photo of the surviving Carthage amphitheatre monument; current remains cannot illustrate the intact arena or a specific martyrdom event. Bomgardner’s AJA abstract argues initial construction in late 1st/early 2nd century and major rebuilding shortly after 165, but full article was not accessible (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.2307/505400). The picture does not prove the Perpetua/Felicity martyrdom location; avoid tying the depicted building to that event as fact. Credit author, link license, indicate modifications, and share adaptations under compatible BY-SA terms.

researchNotes: Lugdunum’s official museum site states the theatre underwent modifications, became a quarry after abandonment, and was excavated/partly reconstructed in the first half of the 20th century; present form is not an unchanged ancient view.
UNESCO lists Carthage as a multi-period archaeological property and identifies the Roman theatre, amphitheatre and Antonine baths among its components.

The Carthage amphitheatre chronology comes only from the accessible abstract of Bomgardner 1989; full paper not read. It proposes late 1st/early 2nd-century construction and rebuilding shortly after 165.
